arXiv:1903.02541v1 [cs.LG] 06 Mar 2019

Relational Pooling for Graph Representations

Ryan L. Murphy Affiliation: Department of Statistics, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA    Balasubramaniam Srinivasan Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA    Vinayak Rao Affiliation: Department of Statistics, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA    Bruno Ribeiro Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA Correspondence to: murph213@purdue.edu
Abstract

This work generalizes graph neural networks (GNNs) beyond those based on the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) algorithm, graph Laplacians, and graph diffusion kernels. Our approach, denoted Relational Pooling (RP), draws from the theory of finite partial exchangeability to provide a framework with maximal representation power for graphs. RP can work with existing graph representation models, and somewhat counterintuitively, can make them even more powerful than the original WL isomorphism test. Additionally, RP is the first theoretically sound framework to use architectures like Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for graph classification. RP also has graph kernels as a special case. We demonstrate improved performance of novel RP-based graph representations over current state-of-the-art methods on a number of tasks.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Applications with relational graph data, such as molecule classification, social and biological network predictions, first order logic, and natural language understanding, require an effective representation of graph structures and their attributes. Representation learning for graph data has made tremendous progress in recent years. However, current schemes are unable to produce so-called most-powerful representations, which can provably distinguish all distinct graphs, up to graph isomorphisms. Consider the broad class of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) based Graph Neural Networks (WL-GNNs), for instance (Xu et al., 2019; Gilmer et al., 2017; Duvenaud et al., 2015; Kipf & Welling, 2016; Hamilton et al., 2017a; Velickovic et al., 2017; Monti et al., 2017; Ying et al., 2018). These cannot give distinct representations for graphs that cannot be distinguished by the standard WL isomorphism test (Cai et al., 1992; Xu et al., 2019). As graph neural networks are applied to increasingly more challenging problems, having a most-powerful framework for graph representation learning would be a key development in geometric deep learning (Bronstein et al., 2017).

In this work we introduce Relational Pooling (RP), a novel framework for graph neural networks that has provably maximal representation power for any graph input. While current approaches are mostly bottom-up, specified procedurally through transformations on graphs, RP takes a top-down approach, specifying an idealized most-powerful representation for graphs and then a framework to develop algorithms to approximate this ideal. The RP ideal can distinguish graphs not distinguishable by the WL isomorphism test, and, more surprisingly, we show that under the RP framework, practical algorithms based on WL-GNNs can be made to distinguish graphs not distinguishable by their corresponding WL-isomorphism test.

RP views relational learning as a pooling operation with partial invariances (graph isomorphism invariances), a framework inspired by the partial exchangeability of graph data (Aldous, 1981; Diaconis & Janson, 2008; Orbanz & Roy, 2015). RP differs from these earlier works by its focus on learning representations of finite but variable-size graphs. In particular, the RP function acts on a finite but arbitrary-sized graph GG, which may be endowed with vertex or edge attributes, and outputs a single representation of the input, f¯¯​(G)\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G), that is invariant to graph isomorphisms. Transductive and inductive models are both possible in RP, though in this paper, we will focus on inductive whole-graph embeddings to simplify our exposition.

Contributions. We make the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    We introduce Relational Pooling (RP), a novel framework for graph representation that can be combined with any existing neural network architecture, including ones not generally associated with graphs such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs).

  2. 2.

    We prove that RP has maximal representation power for any graph input. We also show that WL-GNNs combined with RP (denoted RP-GNN) have more representation power than the WL test (or existing WL-GNNs). In our experiments, we classify graphs that cannot be distinguished by the standard WL test and an existing WL-GNN (Xu et al., 2019).

  3. 3.

    We introduce approximation approaches to make RP tractable. We demonstrate empirically that these approximations to the RP ideal still lead to strong performance and that combining RP-GNN with our tractability strategies can speed up graph classification tasks when compared to traditional WL-GNNs.

2 Relational Pooling

Notation.

Let G=(V,E,𝑿(v),𝑿(e))G=(V,E,{\bm{X}}^{(v)},{\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(e)}) be an attributed graph, where 𝑿(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)} is a |V|×dv|V|\times d_{v} matrix representing node attributes and 𝑿(e){\bm{\mathsfit{X}}}^{(e)} is a |V|×|V|×de|V|\times|V|\times d_{e} tensor representing edge attributes. W.l.o.g. the vertices are sequentially indexed: V={1,…,|V|}V=\{1,\ldots,|V|\}. A permutation is a bijective function on the vertex indices π:V→V\pi:V\to V and the set of all permutations Π|V|\Pi_{|V|} contains all such distinct mappings π\pi. By definition, a permutation of VV does not alter the connectivity structure or attributes of a graph, thus we desire functions thereof to be permutation-invariant, or isomorphic-invariant.

Throughout this work we represent GG by two data structures: (1) a |V|×|V|×(1+de)|V|\times|V|\times(1+d_{e}) tensor that combines GG’s adjacency matrix with its edge attributes and (2) a |V|×dv|V|\times d_{v} matrix representing node attributes 𝑿(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)}. The tensor is defined as 𝑨v,u,⋅=[𝟙(v,u)∈E⨝Xv,u(e)]{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{v,u,\cdot}=\left[\mathbb{1}_{(v,u)\in E}\Join{\mathsfit{X}}^{(e)}_{v,u}\right] for v,u∈{1,2,…,|V|}v,u\in\{1,2,\ldots,|V|\} where [⋅⨝⋅]\left[\cdot\Join\cdot\right] denotes concatenation along the 3rd mode of the tensor, 𝟙(⋅)\mathbb{1}_{(\cdot)} denotes the indicator function, and Xv,u(e){\mathsfit{X}}^{(e)}_{v,u} denotes the attributes of edge (v,u)(v,u) by a slight abuse of notation. Here, a (joint) permutation over the node indices is represented by 𝑨π,π{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi} defined as (𝑨π,π)π⁡(i),π⁡(j),k=Ai,j,k({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi})_{\pi(i),\pi(j),k}={\mathsfit{A}}_{i,j,k} and by 𝑿π(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi} defined as (𝑿π(v))π⁡(i),l=Xi,l(v)({\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi})_{\pi(i),l}={X}^{(v)}_{i,l}, ∀i,j∈V\forall i,j\in V, k∈{1,…,1+de}k\in\{1,\ldots,1+d_{e}\}, l∈{1,…,dv}l\in\{1,\ldots,d_{v}\}. Additional details and examples can be found in the Supplementary Material. Kearnes et al. (2016) shows a similar representation.

Joint RP.

Inspired by joint exchangeability (Aldous, 1981; Diaconis & Janson, 2008; Orbanz & Roy, 2015), joint RP defines isomorphic-invariant functions over non-bipartite graphs, whether with directed or undirected edges, as

f¯¯​(G)=1|V|!​∑π∈Π|V|f⇀(𝑨π,π,𝑿π(v)),\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G)=\frac{1}{|V|!}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{|V|}}\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi},{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}), (1)

where f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} is an arbitrary (and possibly permutation-sensitive) function of the adjacency tensor and node attributes. We use the double-bar notation ⋅¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$\cdot$}}} to denote a function that is invariant to any permutation π\pi, following Murphy et al. (2019). Since equation 1 averages over all valid permutations, it is easy to see that f¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}} is an isomorphic-invariant function and can theoretically represent any such function g¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$g$}}} (consider f⇀=g¯¯\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}=\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$g$}}}). Note that we can compose f¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}} with another function ρ\rho (outside the summation) to capture additional signal in the input (Murphy et al., 2019). This construction can give a maximally expressive graph representation (Theorem 2.1) that is intractable. In later sections we consider various neural network architectures for f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} and approaches to make the sum in equation 1 tractable.

Separate RP.

In a bipartite graph (e.g., consumers ×\times products) VV is composed of two disjoint sets V(r)V^{(\text{r})} and V(c)V^{(\text{c})}, requiring separate exchangeability (Diaconis & Janson, 2008; Orbanz & Roy, 2015). Separate RP is defined for bipartite graphs to preserve separate invariance:

f¯¯​(G)=C​∑π(r)∈Π|V(r)|∑π(c)∈Π|V(c)|f⇀(Gπ(r),π(c))=C​∑π(r)∈Π|V(r)|∑π(c)∈Π|V(c)|f⇀(𝑨π(r),π(c),Xπ(r)(r,v),Xπ(c)(c,v)),\begin{split}\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G)&=C\sum_{\pi^{\text{(r)}}\in\Pi_{|V^{\text{(r)}}|}}\sum_{\pi^{\text{(c)}}\in\Pi_{|V^{\text{(c)}}|}}\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}(G_{\pi^{\text{(r)}},\pi^{\text{(c)}}})\\ &=C\sum_{\pi^{\text{(r)}}\in\Pi_{|V^{\text{(r)}}|}}\sum_{\pi^{\text{(c)}}\in\Pi_{|V^{\text{(c)}}|}}\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}\big({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi^{\text{(r)}},\pi^{\text{(c)}}},X_{\pi^{\text{(r)}}}^{(\text{r},v)},X_{\pi^{\text{(c)}}}^{(\text{c},v)}\big),\\ \end{split} (2)

where C=(|V(r)|!​|V(c)|!)−1C=(|V^{\text{(r)}}|!\,|V^{\text{(c)}}|!)^{-1}, π(r)\pi^{\text{(r)}} and π(c)\pi^{\text{(c)}} are permutations of the rows and columns, respectively, and 𝑿π(r)(r,v){\bm{X}}_{\pi^{\text{(r)}}}^{(\text{r},v)} and 𝑿π(c)(c,v){\bm{X}}_{\pi^{\text{(c)}}}^{(\text{c},v)} denote permutations of the attributes of V(r)V^{(\text{r})} and V(c)V^{(\text{c})}, respectively. All of our results that apply to joint RP also apply to separate RP.

2.1 Representation Power of RP

Theorem 2.1.

If node and edge attributes come from a finite set, then the representation f¯¯​(G)\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G) in equation 1 is the most expressive representation of GG, provided f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} is sufficiently expressive (e.g., a universal approximator).

All proofs are shown in the Supplementary Material. Theorem 2.1 shows that RP can be used to solve any graph-related regression or classification problem over finite graphs with finite attributes, including the problem of graph isomorphism (gives graph fingerprints that are unique between nonisomorphic graphs and shared between isomorphic graphs). The proof provides a key insight into the formulation of RP; a practitioner can focus on building highly expressive functions f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} that need not be isomorphic-invariant, and the RP summation assures that isomorphic-invariance is satisfied.

2.2 Neural Network Architectures

By allowing f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} to be permutation sensitive, RP allows the use of a wide range of neural network architectures, some of which we describe below.

RNNs, MLPs. A valid architecture to compute equation 1 is to vectorize the graph (concatenating node attributes with edge attributes) and learn f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} over the resulting sequence. The function f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} can be a recurrent neural network, like an LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) or GRU (Cho et al., 2014), or a fixed-input function like a feedforward neural network (multilayer perceptron, MLP) with padding if the sequences have different sizes. Concretely,

f¯¯​(G)\displaystyle\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G) =1|V|!​∑π∈Π|V|f⇀(vec⁡(𝑨π,π,𝑿π(v))).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|V|!}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{|V|}}\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}\big(\mathrm{vec}({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi},{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi})\big).

Please refer to section A in the Supplementary Material for more details on the vec\mathrm{vec} vectorization operator.

CNNs. Convolutional neural networks can also be directly applied over the tensor 𝑨π,π{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi} and combined with the node features 𝑿π(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}, as in

f¯¯(G)=1|V|!∑π∈Π|V|MLP([CNN(𝑨π,π)⨝MLP(𝑿π(v))]),\!\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G)\!=\!\frac{1}{|V|!}\!\!\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{|V|}}\mathrm{MLP}\bigg(\left[\mathrm{CNN}({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi})\Join\mathrm{MLP}({\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi})\right]\bigg), (3)

where CNN is a 2D convolutional neural network (LeCun et al., 1989; Krizhevsky et al., 2012) if there are no edge features and a 3D convolutional neural network (Ji et al., 2013) if there are edge features, [⋅⨝⋅]\left[\cdot\Join\cdot\right] is a concatenation of the representations, and MLP is a feedforward network (multilayer perceptron). The 3D CNN will often need to ensure that variable-sized graphs are mapped into the same sized representation. This can be achieved by multi-resolution 3D convolutions (Qi et al., 2016).

GNNs. The function f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} can also be a graph neural network, a broad class of models which uses the graph GG itself to define the computation graph. The models we consider follow a message-passing (Gilmer et al., 2017), or neighborhood aggregation, framework defined by the recursion

𝐡u(l)=ϕ⁡(𝐡u(l−1),JP​((𝐡v(l−1))v∈𝒩⁡(u))),{\bf h}^{(l)}_{u}=\phi\left({\bf h}^{(l-1)}_{u},\text{JP}\big(({\bf h}^{(l-1)}_{v})_{v\in{\mathcal{N}}(u)}\big)\right), (4)

where ϕ\phi is a learnable function, JP is a general (learnable) permutation-invariant function (Murphy et al., 2019), 𝒩⁡(u){\mathcal{N}}(u) is the set of neighbors of u∈Vu\in V, and 𝐡u(l)∈ℝdh(l){\bf h}^{(l)}_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}^{(l)}} is a vector describing the embedding of node uu at layer 1≤l≤L1\leq l\leq L of the computation graph (𝐡u(0){\bf h}^{(0)}_{u} is defined as the uthu^{\text{th}} row of 𝑿(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)}). Under this framework, vertex embeddings can be used directly to predict vertex-level targets, or all vertex embeddings can be aggregated (via a learnable function) to form an embedding 𝐡G{\bf h}_{G} used for graph-wide tasks. Xu et al. (2019) showed that these architectures can be at most as powerful as the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) algorithm for testing graph isomorphism (Weisfeiler & Lehman, 1968), which itself effectively follows a message-passing scheme. Accordingly, we will broadly refer to models following the message-passing scheme defined by equation 4 as WL-GNNs.

There are a number of variations of equation 4 in the literature. Among the earliest was Duvenaud et al. (2015), who proposed using embeddings from all layers l∈{1,2,…,L}l\in\{1,2,\ldots,L\} for graph classification. Hamilton et al. (2017a) extended the framework to node classification and link prediction tasks, using the embedding at the last layer, while Xu et al. (2018) extend Hamilton et al. (2017a) by once again considering all embeddings at all layers for node and link prediction tasks. Other variations include attention (Velickovic et al., 2018) and similar improvements. An interesting perspective is that approximate spectral graph convolutions can be shown to yield models of this form (for instance, (Kipf & Welling, 2016)). Recently, Xu et al. (2019) propose an architecture called Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) that they show to be as powerful as the WL test in representing isomorphic and nonisomorphic graphs with discrete attributes. More GNN models are discussed in section 3.

It might appear that there is no gain in using a WL-GNN for f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} as it is invariant to π\pi, collapsing the sum of equation 1 into a single term. There are, however, two main advantages: (1) it allows WL-GNNs to be more powerful than the WL isomorphism test if we make f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} permutation sensitive such as in the manner we describe below, and (2) it gives us a theoretically sound procedure to apply a WL-GNN over smaller random subgraphs of the original graph, rather than the entire graph, significantly speeding up GNNs. We will revisit (2) when we delve into tractability approaches to RP using kk-ary dependencies.

Can a WL-GNN be more powerful than the WL test?

WL-GNNs have a representation shortcoming that they inherit from the WL test  (Arvind et al., 2017; Cai et al., 1992; Fürer, 2017). The node representation in a WL-GNN is incapable of encoding whether two nodes have the same neighbor or distinct neighbors with the same attributes. Consider a graph task where graphs represent molecules, with vertex attributes indicating the atom type and edges denoting the presence or absence of bonds. Here, the first WL-GNN layer is incapable of distinguishing that two (say) carbon atoms have a bond with the same carbon atom, or a bond to two distinct carbon atoms. As we move up the layers of the WL-GNN, node representations become node features in succeeding layers, and the hope is that eventually nodes get unique representations (up to isomorphisms), which would allow the WL-GNN to detect whether or not two nodes have the same neighbor based on the unique features of their neighbors.

However, if the WL-GNN does not have enough layers to guarantee unique node representations (up to isomorphisms) or if the graph has complex cycles, the WL-GNN will fail to correctly represent the graph and its nodes. To better understand this challenge, consider an extreme case illustrated with the two graphs in figure 1. These are cycle graphs with M=11M=11 nodes and skip links of different lengths around the circle R∈{2,3}R\in\{2,3\} added to all pairs of vertices. These highly symmetric graphs are instances of circulant graphs and are well-known in the graph theory literature (Sethuraman, 2004). The two graphs are clearly distinct (nonisomorphic) but the WL algorithm – and thus any WL-GNN – is incapable of representing the nodes in the left graph distinctly from nodes in the right graph. Note that the vertex attributes are assumed to be initialized as hu(0)=ch^{(0)}_{u}=c, where cc is some constant (usually 1, w.l.o.g.).

RP offers a flexible approach to make WL-GNN more expressive than its WL test. Let f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} be a WL-GNN that we make permutation sensitive by assigning each node an extra node attribute, such as a vertex identifier, that depends on π\pi. Intuitively, vertex identifiers help distinguish neighbors that otherwise appear identical and mitigate the problem illustrated by our ‘carbon atoms’ example above. In particular, the node in the vv-th vertex in the permuted graph is assigned a one-hot encoding, which can be represented by augmenting the vertex attribute matrix to obtain [𝑿π(v)⨝I|V|]\left[{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}\Join I_{|V|}\right], where I|V|I_{|V|} is a |V|×|V||V|\times|V| identity matrix and [B⨝C]\left[B\Join C\right] concatenates the columns of matrices BB and CC. RP-GNN is then given by

f¯¯​(G)\displaystyle\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G) =1|V|!∑π∈Π|V|f⇀(𝑨π,π,[𝑿π(v)⨝I|V|])\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|V|!}\!\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{|V|}}\!\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}\left({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi},\left[{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}\Join I_{|V|}\right]\right) (5)
=1|V|!∑π∈Π|V|f⇀(𝑨,[𝑿(v)⨝(I|V|)π]),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|V|!}\!\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{|V|}}\!\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}\left({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}},\left[{\bm{X}}^{(v)}\Join(I_{|V|})_{\pi}\right]\right),

where the second holds since f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} is an isomorphic-invariant GNN. Equation 5 is permutation-invariant while all nodes are guaranteed to have unique attributes. The following theorem proves that f¯¯​(G)\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G) in equation 5 is strictly more expressive than the original WL-GNN in that it can distinguish all nodes and graphs that WL-GNN can in addition to graphs that the original WL-GNN cannot. We provide further details on this formulation in the Supplementary Material.

Theorem 2.2.

The RP-GNN in equation 5 is strictly more expressive than the original WL-GNN. Specifically, if f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} is a GIN (Xu et al., 2019) and the graph has discrete attributes, its RP-GNN is more powerful than the WL test.

The power of RP-GNN in equation 5 comes at a heavy computational cost. Fortunately, there multiple ways to make equation 5 tractable while still retaining some of the power of RP-GNNs over standard GNNs. We leave tractability approaches that are common to other architectures to section 2.3. One approach that is specific to RP-GNN on attributed graphs adds just enough unique new ids to GG to ensure that all node attributes in the graph are unique, reducing the number of permutations in equation 5. In a molecule, such as Hydroxyformaldehyde C​H2​O2CH_{2}O_{2}, we only need to give extra ids to make atoms unique: (C,1)(C,1), (H,1)(H,1), (H,2)(H,2), (O,1)(O,1), (O,2)(O,2). Now, only a total of 1!⋅2!⋅2!=41!\cdot 2!\cdot 2!=4 permutations need to be considered in equation 5. An approximation, useful for unattributed graphs, assigns id imodmi\!\!\mod m to node ii, where m=1m=1 is the original GNN and m=|V|m=|V| is the most powerful RP-GNN.

2.3 RP Tractability

2.3.1 Tractability through canonical orientations

By itself equation 1 is intractable, and calls for approximations of some sort. The most direct approach towards this is to compose a permutation-sensitive f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} with a canonical orientation function that re-orders 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}} such that CANONICAL​(𝑨,𝑿(v))=CANONICAL​(𝑨π,π,𝑿π(v))\text{CANONICAL}({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}},{\bm{X}}^{(v)})=\text{CANONICAL}({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi},{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}), ∀π∈Π|V|\forall\pi\in\Pi_{|V|}. This causes the sum over all permutations to collapse to just an evaluation of f⇀∘CANONICAL\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}\circ\text{CANONICAL}. Essentially, this introduces a fixed component into the permutation invariant function f¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}, with only the second stage learned from data. Note that this is not equivalent to the original problem as the CANONICAL function need not have learnable parameters (e.g. sorting by centrality scores). Such an approach is however only as useful as its canonical orientation, which if not strongly correlated with the objective function, can result in poor representations. Consider a scenario where we order nodes according to their degrees (breaking ties according to some rule) and suppose that the objective function is correlated with the vertex attributes but independent of vertex degrees. Effectively, this canonical orientation forms a single permutation of the vertex attribute matrix–likely differing from graph to graph–learning with which can result in poor task performance.

A more flexible approach collapses the set of all permutations into a much smaller set of equivalent permutations. We denote this approach poly-canonical orientation. Depth-First Search (DFS) and Breadth-First Search (BFS) node orderings are two examples of poly-canonical orientations. In a DFS, the nodes of the adjacency matrix/tensor 𝑨π,π{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi} are ordered 1 to |V||V| according to the order they are visited by a DFS starting at π⁡(1)\pi(1). Thus, if GG is a length-three path and we consider permutation functions defined (elementwise) as π⁡(1,2,3)=(1,2,3)\pi(1,2,3)=(1,2,3) and π′​(1,2,3)=(1,3,2)\pi^{\prime}(1,2,3)=(1,3,2), our DFS or BFS would see respectively and (where vertices are numbered by permuted indices), start at π⁡(1)=1\pi(1)=1 and result in the same left-to-right sorting for both permutations. If the graph is disconnected, the search starts at the first node of each connected component. Note that beyond the starting node, the search traversal order of neighbors of a node also depends on π\pi. Learning canonical orders from data is a discrete optimization problem left for future work.

2.3.2 Tractability through π\pi-SGD

The key approach to achieve tractable joint and separate RP is to sample random permutations during training. This approach offers the significant computational savings of a single canonical ordering while being considerably more flexible and robust, and avoids the need to learn a good canonical ordering for a given objective function.

For simplicity, we analyze the optimization with a single sampled permutation in a supervised graph classification setting, but this can be easily extended to sampling multiple permutations and unsupervised settings. Further, while we focus on joint invariance, the formulation is similar for separate invariance. Consider NN training data examples 𝒟≡{(G⁡(1),𝒚⁡(1)),…,(G⁡(N),𝒚⁡(N))}\mathcal{D}\equiv\{(G(1),{\bm{y}}(1)),\ldots,(G(N),{\bm{y}}(N))\}, where 𝒚⁡(i)∈𝕐{\bm{y}}(i)\in{\mathbb{Y}} is the target output and graph G⁡(i)G(i) its corresponding graph input. For a parameterized function f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} with parameters 𝑾{\bm{W}},

f¯¯​(G⁡(i),𝑾)=1|V⁡(i)|!​∑π∈Π|V⁡(i)|f⇀(𝑨π,π​(i),𝑿π(v)​(i),𝑾),\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G(i);{\bm{W}})=\frac{1}{|V(i)|!}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{|V(i)|}}\hskip 0.0pt\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi}(i),{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}(i);{\bm{W}}),

our goal is to minimize the empirical loss

L¯¯​(𝒟,𝑾)=∑i=1NL⁡(𝒚⁡(i),f¯¯​(G⁡(i),𝑾)),\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$L$}}}(\mathcal{D};{\bm{W}})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\!L\left({\bm{y}}(i)\,,\,\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G(i);{\bm{W}})\right), (6)

where LL is a convex loss function of f¯¯​(⋅,⋅)\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(\cdot;\cdot) such as cross-entropy, negative log-likelihood, or square loss. Now, for each graph G⁡(i)G(i) a random permutation 𝐬i{\mathbf{s}}_{i} is sampled uniformly as 𝐬i∼{\mathbf{s}}_{i}\sim Unif​(Π|V⁡(i)|)\text{Unif}(\Pi_{|V(i)|}), and we consider replacing the RP sum in equation 1 with the estimate

f¯¯^​(G𝐬i,𝐬i​(i),𝑾)=f⇀(𝑨𝐬i,𝐬i​(i),𝑿𝐬i(v)​(i),𝑾),\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i);{\bm{W}})=\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i),{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i);{\bm{W}}), (7)

where we have introduced the notation Gsi,si​(i)G_{s_{i},s_{i}}(i) to denote a permutation of the corresponding tensor 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}} and matrix 𝑿(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)}. Note that, for separate invariance, we would write Gsi,si′​(i)G_{s_{i},s_{i}^{\prime}}(i) to indicate that one distinct permutation is sampled for each set of vertices. The estimator in equation 7 is unbiased: E𝐬i​[f¯¯^​(G𝐬i,𝐬i​(i),𝑾)]=f¯¯​(G⁡(i),𝑾)E_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}[\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i);{\bm{W}})]=\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G(i);{\bm{W}}). Note however that when f¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}} is chained with a nonlinear loss LL, the composition is no longer unbiased: E𝐬i​[L⁡(𝒚⁡(i),f¯¯^​(G𝐬i,𝐬i​(i),𝑾))]≠L⁡(𝒚⁡(i),E𝐬i​[f¯¯^​(G𝐬i,𝐬i​(i),𝑾)])E_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}[L({\bm{y}}(i),\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i);{\bm{W}}))]\neq L({\bm{y}}(i),E_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}[\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i);{\bm{W}})]). Nevertheless, as we will soon justify, we follow Murphy et al. (2019) and use this estimate in our optimization, calling the resulting procedure π\pi-SGD for RP:

Definition 2.1 (π\pi-SGD for RP).

Let ℬt={(G⁡(1),𝐲⁡(1)),…,(G⁡(B),𝐲⁡(B))}{\mathcal{B}}_{t}=\{(G(1),{\bm{y}}(1)),\ldots,(G(B),{\bm{y}}(B))\} be a mini-batch i.i.d. sampled uniformly from the training data 𝒟\mathcal{D} at step tt. Consider the stochastic gradient descent update

𝑾t=𝑾t−1−ηt​𝐙t,{\bm{W}}_{t}={\bm{W}}_{t-1}-\eta_{t}{\mathbf{Z}}_{t}, (8)

where 𝐙t=1B​∑i=1B∇𝐖L​(𝐲⁡(i),f¯¯^​(G𝐬i,𝐬i​(i),𝐖t−1)){\mathbf{Z}}_{t}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\nabla_{{\bm{W}}}L\left({\bm{y}}(i),\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i);{\bm{W}}_{t-1})\right) is the random gradient with the random permutations {𝐬i}i=1B\{{\mathbf{s}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}, (sampled independently 𝐬i∼Uniform​(Π|V⁡(i)|){\mathbf{s}}_{i}\sim\text{Uniform}(\Pi_{|V(i)|}) for all graphs G⁡(i)G(i) in batch ℬt{\mathcal{B}}_{t}), and the learning rate is ηt∈(0,1)\eta_{t}\in(0,1) s.t. limt→∞ηt=0\lim_{t\to\infty}\eta_{t}=0, ∑t=1∞ηt=∞\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}=\infty, and ∑t=1∞ηt2<∞\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}^{2}<\infty.

Effectively, this is a Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation algorithm of gradient descent (Robbins & Monro, 1951; Bottou, 2012) and optimizes the following modified objective:

J¯¯(𝒟;𝑾)=1N​∑i=1NE𝐬i​[L⁡(𝒚⁡(i),f¯¯^​(G𝐬i,𝐬i​(i),𝑾))]=1N​∑i=1N1|V⁡(i)|!​∑π∈Π|V⁡(i)|L⁡(𝒚⁡(i),f¯¯^​(Gπ,π​(i),𝑾)).\begin{split}\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$J$}}}&(\mathcal{D};{\bm{W}})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}E_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}\left[\!L\Bigg({\bm{y}}(i),\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i);{\bm{W}})\Bigg)\right]\\ &=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{|V(i)|!}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{|V(i)|}}L\Bigg({\bm{y}}(i),\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{\pi,\pi}(i);{\bm{W}})\Bigg).\end{split} (9)

Observe that the expectation over permutations is now outside the loss function (recall f¯¯​(G​(i),𝑾)\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G(i);{\bm{W}}) in in equation 6 is an expectation). As in equation 6, the loss in equation 9 is also permutation-invariant, though we note that π\pi-SGD, after a finite number of iterations, returns a f¯¯^​(G𝐬i,𝐬i​(i),𝑾)\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i);{\bm{W}}) sensitive to the random input permutations of G𝐬i,𝐬i​(i)G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{i},{\mathbf{s}}_{i}}(i) presented to the algorithm. Further, unless the function f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} itself is permutation-invariant (f¯¯=f⇀\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}=\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}), the optima of J¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$J$}}} are different from those of the original objective function L¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$L$}}}. Instead, if LL is convex in f¯¯​(⋅,⋅)\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(\cdot;\cdot), J¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$J$}}} is an upper bound to L¯¯\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$L$}}} via Jensen’s inequality, and minimizing this upper bound forms a tractable surrogate to the original RP objective in equation 6.

The next result draws on the π\pi-SGD formulation of Murphy et al. (2019) showing the convergence properties of our stochastic optimization.

Proposition 2.1.

[π\pi-SGD Convergence (Murphy et al., 2019)] The optimization of π\pi-SGD enjoys properties of almost sure convergence to the optimal 𝐖{\bm{W}} under similar conditions as SGD.

Given fixed point 𝑾⋆{\bm{W}}^{\star} of the π\pi-SGD optimization and a new graph GG at inference time, we may opt to exactly compute E𝐬​[f¯¯^​(G𝐬,𝐬,𝑾⋆)]=f¯¯​(G,𝑾⋆)E_{{\mathbf{s}}}[\hat{\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}}(G_{{\mathbf{s}},{\mathbf{s}}};{\bm{W}}^{\star})]=\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}(G;{\bm{W}}^{\star}) or estimate it with 1m​∑j=1mf⇀(G𝐬j,𝐬j;𝑾⋆)\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}(G_{{\mathbf{s}}_{j},{\mathbf{s}}_{j}};{\bm{W}}^{\star}) where 𝐬1​…,𝐬m​∼i.i.d.​Uniform​(Π|V|){\mathbf{s}}_{1}\ldots,{\mathbf{s}}_{m}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\text{Uniform}\big(\Pi_{|V|}\big).

2.3.3 Tractability through kk-ary dependencies

In Murphy et al. (2019), the authors propose kk-ary pooling wherein computational complexity is reduced from summing over all permutations of the input sequence to just subsequences of size kk. In the context of statistical Markov Random Field models, exchangeability assumptions also provide a type of kk-ary tractability (Niepert & Van den Broeck, 2014). Inspired by this, we propose kk-ary Relational Pooling which operates on kk-node induced subgraphs of GG. This corresponds to patches of size k×k×(de+1)k\times k\times(d_{e}+1) of 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}} and kk rows of 𝑿(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)}. Formally, we define kk-ary RP in joint RP by

f¯¯(k)(G;𝑾)=1|V|!∑π∈Π|V|f⇀(𝑨π,π[:k,:k,:],𝑿π(v)[:k,:];𝑾),\ \overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}^{(k)}\!\!(G;{\bm{W}})\!=\!\frac{1}{|V|!}\!\sum_{\pi\!\in\Pi_{|V|}}\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}\!\Big(\!{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi}[1\!\!:\!\!k,1\!\!:\!\!k,:],{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}[1\!\!:\!\!k,\!:];{\bm{W}}\Big), (10)

where 𝑨⁡[⋅,⋅,⋅]{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}[\cdot,\cdot,\cdot] denotes access to elements in the first, second, and third modes of 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}; a:ba\!\!:\!\!b denotes selecting elements corresponding to indices from aa to bb inclusive; and “::” by itself denotes all elements along a mode. Thus, we permute the adjacency tensor and select edge-attribute fibers along the third mode from the upper left k×k×(de+1)k\times k\times(d_{e}+1) subtensor of 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}} as well as the vertex attributes from the first kk rows of 𝑿π(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}. In practice, the relevant kk-node induced subgraphs can be selected without permuting the entire tensor 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}} and matrix 𝑿(v){\bm{X}}^{(v)}. Separate RP needs two values k1k_{1} and k2k_{2}, representing the number of vertices to be selected from each partite set as inputs, respectively.

An illustration of the joint kk-ary RP is depicted in figure 2 over a 5-node undirected graph GG with no vertex features. The graph is represented on the right with its original node indices shown. Its corresponding adjacency tensor 𝑨π†,π†{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi^{\dagger},\pi^{\dagger}} with permutation π†​(1,2,3,4,5)=(3,4,1,2,5)\pi^{\dagger}(1,2,3,4,5)=(3,4,1,2,5) is shown on the left, depicted as a cube whose depth depicts the adjacency matrix (front matrix slice) and a one-dimensional edge feature (back matrix slice), and its first and second modes the five nodes in the graph. The first representation shows a shaded 3×3×(1+de)3\times 3\times(1+d_{e}) region where elements of 𝑨π†,π†{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi^{\dagger},\pi^{\dagger}} are considered as input to f⇀(3)\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}^{(3)} in a 3-ary joint RP. The highlighted nodes and edges on the right shows the corresponding 33-node induced subgraph in GG. More generally, we can make the following conclusion:

Proposition 2.2.

The RP in equation 10 requires summing over all kk-node induced subgraphs of GG, thus saving computation when k<|V|k<|V|, reducing the number of terms in the sum from |V|!|V|! to |V|!(|V|−k)!\frac{|V|!}{(|V|-k)!}.

Even fewer computations are needed if f⇀(k)\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}^{(k)} is made permutation-invariant over its input (a kk-node induced subgraph).

We now show that the set of kk-ary RP functions is strictly more expressive than the set of (k−1)(k\!\!-\!\!1)-ary RP functions, 1<k≤|V|1<k\leq|V|.

Proposition 2.3.

f¯¯(k)\overline{\overline{\lower 0.86108pt\hbox{$f$}}}^{(k)} becomes strictly more expressive as kk increases. That is, for any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, define ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} as the set of all permutation-invariant graph functions that can be represented by RP with kk-ary dependencies. Then, ℱk−1\mathcal{F}_{k-1} is a proper subset of ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} if k≤|V|k\leq|V|. Thus, RP with kk-ary dependencies can express any RP function with (k−1)(k-1)-ary dependencies, but the converse does not hold.

Further computational savings.

Even over moderately-sized graphs, the number of kk-node induced subgraphs can be very large. Here we propose approaches for further computational savings.

Ignoring disconnected subgraphs: In some applications, we may want to define f⇀(𝑨π,π,…)=0\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi},\ldots)~=~0 for any permutation π\pi whose first kk nodes form a disconnected kk-node induced subgraph in GG. In sparse graphs, the number of disconnected kk-node induced subgraphs is orders of magnitude larger than the number of connected subgraphs, making this f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} assumption bear out tremendous computational benefits.

Use of π\pi-SGD: Here, we can combine the kk-ary approximation with other computational savings such as π\pi-SGD and poly-canonical orientations. For instance, a forward pass can consist of sampling a random starting vertex, performing a BFS orientation of 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}, and selecting the left corner k×k×(de+1)k\times k\times(d_{e}+1) block of 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}} (which is a connected induced subgraph by virtue of the BFS). The BFS does not need to be run over the entire graph. This approach, however, will be biased and unable to consider all possible connected induced subgraphs. An unbiased estimate over connected induced subgraphs can be achieved with the MCMC finite-sample unbiased estimator of Teixeira et al. (2018).

Graph kernels as special cases of kk-ary RP.

Graph kernels of Yanardag & Vishwanathan (2015) are special cases of kk-ary RP where we assume node and edge attributes are discrete and we hand-pick the f⇀(𝑨π,π[:k,:k,:],𝑿π(v)[:k,:])\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}(\!{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi}[1\!\!:\!\!k,1\!\!:\!\!k,:],{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}[1\!\!:\!\!k,\!:]) as a one-hot encoding over the input kk-node subgraph 𝑨π,π[:k,:k,:]{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{\pi,\pi}[1\!\!:\!\!k,1\!\!:\!\!k,:] with attributes 𝑿π(v)[:k,:]{\bm{X}}^{(v)}_{\pi}[1\!\!:\!\!k,\!:]. The sum over all permutations will be k!k! times the frequency of kk-node subgraphs, which is the basis of Yanardag & Vishwanathan (2015).

3 Related Work

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) form an increasingly popular class of methods (Xu et al., 2019; Gilmer et al., 2017; Bruna et al., 2013; Niepert et al., 2016; Defferrard et al., 2016; Duvenaud et al., 2015; Atwood & Towsley, 2016; Kipf & Welling, 2016; Hamilton et al., 2017a; Lee et al., 2018; Velickovic et al., 2017; Monti et al., 2017; Meng et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018; Scarselli et al., 2009). Applications include chemistry, where we may represent a dataset of molecules as a collection of undirected graphs in which vertices represent atoms, edges represent bonds, attributes on edges and/or vertices represent such characteristics as bonding type and charge, and we predict chemical properties like toxicity or photovoltaic efficiency (Gilmer et al., 2017; Duvenaud et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018; Sanchez-Lengeling & Aspuru-Guzik, 2018); document classification wherein a network of documents has vertices representing documents, edges representing citations or hyperlinks, and vertex attributes representing document text (Hamilton et al., 2017b); and many others (cf. Battaglia et al. (2018)).

Recently, Xu et al. (2019) shows that such methods are at most as powerful as the standard Weisfeiler-Lehman algorithm (also known as color refinement or naive vertex classification (Arvind et al., 2017; Fürer, 2017)) for graph isomorphism testing  (Weisfeiler & Lehman, 1968) which fails to distinguish between certain classes of graphs such as regular graphs with the same number of nodes, edges, and degrees (Arvind et al., 2017; Cai et al., 1992; Fürer, 2017). In section 4, we demonstrate this phenomenon and provide empirical evidence that RP can correct some of these shortcomings of WL-GNNs. Higher-order (kk-th order) versions of the Weisfeiler-Lehman isomorphism test WL[kk] do exist (Fürer, 2017), where for WL[2] the algorithm operates on ordered pairs of vertices rather than just vertices. Except for Meng et al. (2018), which introduces a WL[kk]-type graph representation to successfully predict high-order dynamics in temporal graphs, all existing GNNs are based on WL[1]-type isomorphism tests. Higher-order WL tests may be able to give better f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} functions but are outside the scope of this work. We have provided a most-powerful representation and demonstrated that it is more expressive than these WL[1] procedures.

Closer to the RP approach, Montavon et al. (2012) discusses models that use a sorting scheme of a Coulomb matrix for molecules with limited random permutations. However, RP provides a significantly more comprehensive and general framework (with theoretical analysis). Orthogonally, CNNs have been used with graph kernels (Nikolentzos et al., 2018) and some GCNs can be seen as CNNs applied to single canonical orderings (Niepert et al., 2016; Defferrard et al., 2016); RP provides a framework for stochastic optimization over all orderings and over poly-canonical orderings.

In parallel, Bloem-Reddy & Teh (2019) generalizes functions that are invariant to graph permutations to those that are invariant to general group actions, discussing the connections to exchangeable probability distributions (De Finetti, 1937; Aldous, 1981; Diaconis & Janson, 2008). Their theoretical analysis uses a checkerboard function (Orbanz & Roy, 2015) to provide a canonical orientation of the adjacency matrix — that is, a way to map pairs of nonisomorphic graphs to different representations and pairs of isomorphic graphs to the same representation. The translation of these insights into practical algorithms is not yet clear. The canonical orientation cannot be computed in polynomial time unless the graph isormorphism problem can be solved in polynomial time — that is, the use of the left-order canonical orientation algorithm of Ghahramani & Griffiths (2006) proposed by Bloem-Reddy & Teh (2019) will sometimes fail to give a proper canonical orientation for some classes of graphs. Using a single canonical orientation — rather than, say, poly-canonical orientations — also has the same drawbacks as using a single canonical orientation for permutation-invariance over sequence inputs, see the example in Murphy et al. (2019).

4 Experiments

In this section we focus on two types of experiments. The first shows that RP-GNN is more expressive than WL-GNN. The second describes how kk-ary tractability and π\pi-SGD in the RP framework can make WL-GNN more scalable.

4.1 Testing RP-GNN vs WL-GNN

In this section we generalize and perform experiments over the class of graphs represented in figure 1. Here we show that WL-GNNs are necessarily limited in their power to represent the graph structures, and we show how RP can be used to ameliorate or even overcome this limitation. Our experiments compare the RP-GNN of equation 5 using the Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) architecture (Xu et al., 2019) as f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} against the original GIN architecture. We choose GIN because it is arguably the most expressive WL-GNN architecture.

We now generalize the construction of the 44-regular graphs shown in figure 1. Here, the “skip length” RR structural attribute effectively defines an isomorphism class in the sense that predicting RR is tantamount to classifying a graph into its isomorphism class. We are interested in predicting RR as an assessment of RP’s ability to exploit graph structure. Note we do not claim to attempt to solve the graph isomorphism problem since our approach will use approximate learning (π\pi-SGD for RP).

Definition 4.1 (Circulant Skip Links (CSL) graphs).

Consider 4-regular undirected graphs 𝒢skip​(M,R)\mathcal{G}_{\text{skip}}(M,R) such that the MM vertices form a cycle graph (circle) and each vertex is connected to those vertices exactly RR hops away around the circle. Let RR and MM be co-prime natural numbers11 1 Two numbers are co-primes if they share no common factors other than one. such that R<M−1R<M-1. Recursively define the sequence s1=0s_{1}=0, si+1=(si+R)​mod​Ms_{i+1}=(s_{i}+R)\ \mathrm{mod}\ M. We denote by 𝒢skip​(M,R)\mathcal{G}_{\text{skip}}(M,R) the undirected graph whose vertices are {0,1,…,M−1}\{0,1,\ldots,M-1\} and whose edges are consecutive elements in the sequence: (si,si+1)∈E(s_{i},s_{i+1})\in E for any i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}.

Note that there exist R1≠R2R_{1}\neq R_{2} such that 𝒢skip​(M,R1)\mathcal{G}_{\text{skip}}(M,R_{1}) and 𝒢skip​(M,R2)\mathcal{G}_{\text{skip}}(M,R_{2}) are isomorphic, but we are more interested in the cases when they are nonisomorphic.

RP-GIN

Since WL-GNNs are expected to fail at this task, we will define an RP-GNN that we expect to succeed. GIN (Xu et al., 2019) follows the recursive update of equation 4 over LL layers, replacing JP with a summation and defining ϕ\phi as a function that sums its arguments and feeds them through a multilayer perceptron:

𝐡u(l)=MLP(l)​((1+ϵ(l))​𝐡u(l−1)+∑v∈𝒩⁡(u)𝐡v(l−1)),{\bf h}^{(l)}_{u}=\mathrm{MLP}^{(l)}\Big((1+\epsilon^{(l)}){\bf h}^{(l-1)}_{u}+\sum_{v\in{\mathcal{N}}(u)}{\bf h}^{(l-1)}_{v}\Big),

for l=1,…,Ll=1,\ldots,L, where {ϵ(l)}l=1L\{\epsilon^{(l)}\}_{l=1}^{L} can be treated as hyper-parameters or learned parameters. This recursion yields vertex-level representations that can be mapped to a graph-level representation by summing across 𝐡u(l){\bf h}^{(l)}_{u} at each given ll, then concatenating the results, as proposed by Xu et al. (2019). When applying GIN directly on our CSL graphs, we assign a constant vertex attribute to all vertices in keeping with the traditional WL algorithm, as the graph is unattributed. For RP-GIN, we assign unique node attributes by one-hot encoding the vertex ID after permutation, as shown in equation 5. Note that we can only assign such ID attributes to vertices in the RP framework, otherwise it would render GIN permutation sensitive.

Classifying skip lengths.

Now we create a dataset of graphs from {𝒢skip​(41,R)}R\big\{\mathcal{G}_{\text{skip}}(41,R)\big\}_{R} where R∈{2,3,4,5,6,9,11,12,13,16}R\in\{2,3,4,5,6,9,11,12,13,16\} and predict RR as a discrete class label. Note that M=41M=41 is the smallest such that 10 nonisomorphic 𝒢skip​(M,R)\mathcal{G}_{\text{skip}}(M,R) can be formed. From each isomorphism class, we form 14 adjacency matrices by first constructing a matrix A(R)A^{{(R)}} according to the scheme described in definition 4.1 then 13 more as Aπ,π(R)A^{{(R)}}_{\pi,\pi} for 13 distinct permutations π\pi. This gives a balanced dataset of 140 graphs. We evaluate the performance of RP-GIN with five-fold cross validation on this task and also show the performance of standard GIN (with vertex attributes assigned to constant 1) for comparison.

The details of our GIN architecture (which follows Xu et al. (2019)) can be found in the Supplementary Material. RP-GIN uses this architecture as f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} but we use one-hot ids as the vertex features, with m=10m=10 unique IDs. We train with π\pi-SGD, applying one random permutation of each adjacency matrix at each epoch. For inference, we average the score over 15 random permutations, for each graph.

The validation-set accuracies for both models are shown in figure 3. GIN performs no better than random since it yields the same graph representation for every RR. In comparison, RP-GIN yields substantially stronger performance on all folds, demonstrating that RP-GNNs are more powerful than their WL-GNN and serving as empirical validation of Theorem 2.2.

4.2 Predicting Molecular Properties

Application Domain and Datasets.

Deep learning for chemical applications learns functions on raw graph representations of molecules and has a rich literature (Duvenaud et al., 2015; Kearnes et al., 2016; Gilmer et al., 2017). This domain provides challenging tasks on which to evaluate RP, while in other applications, different GNN models often achieve similar performance (Xu et al., 2019; Shchur et al., 2018). We leveraged the MoleculeNet project (Wu et al., 2018), which collects chemical datasets and reports the performance of various models, for choosing our datasets. We chose three on which graph-based models achieved superior performance22 2 Latest results available at http://moleculenet.ai/latest-results, accessed December 2018: HIV, MUV (Rohrer & Baumann, 2009), and Tox21 (Mayr et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016).

These datasets contain measurements on a molecule’s biological activity, ability to inhibit HIV, and qualitative toxicity measurements for the MUV, HIV, and Tox21 datasets, respectively. All response variables are discrete, resulting in classification tasks. The datasets were processed with DeepChem (Ramsundar et al., 2019) and we evaluate all models with ROC-AUC following the MoleculeNet project. All compounds across all datasets are represented by graphs with 75-dimensional vertex (atom) attributes and 14-dimensional edge attributes. An example of a vertex attribute is a one-hot encoding of atom type. The number of molecules and tasks in each dataset is shown in Table 3 in the Supplementary Material.

We evaluate models using RP against the best performing baseline, as reported by MoleculeNet, a model based on the Graph Convolution proposed in Duvenaud et al. (2015) and implemented in DeepChem (by  Altae-Tran et al. (2017)). We also implemented GIN (Xu et al., 2019) but it was unable to outperform the molecule-specialized model of Duvenaud et al. (2015); for instance, this model trains a different weight matrix Wκ(l)W^{(l)}_{\kappa} for each possible degree κ\kappa of a vertex, which would be infeasible in other applications (ϕ\phi in equation 4 is replaced with ϕκ\phi_{\kappa}). We re-trained the DeepChem models using the same number of epochs as the other models we consider to make them more comparable. That being said, many models reached optimal performance before the last epoch; we use the model with best validation-set performance from training for test-set prediction. Our code is available on GitHub33 3 https://github.com/PurdueMINDS/RelationalPooling, and the model architecture, hyperparameters, and training details are discussed in the Supplementary Material.

RP-GNN

Here we evaluate RP-GNN empirically. In particular, we compare the performance of the Duvenaud et al. GNN baseline to RP-Duvenaud, which is defined by equation 5 with f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} represented by the ‘Duvenaud et al.’ model operating on the entire graph. We assign one-hot IDs such that atoms of the same type have unique IDs; see the tractability strategy discussed in section 2.2. We train with π\pi-SGD and sample 20 permutations at inference time. To quantify variability, we train over 20 random folds for Tox21 and HIV and 10 folds for MUV (please see the Supplementary Material for additional details).

The results shown in Table 1 suggest that RP-Duvenaud is more powerful than the baseline on the HIV task and similar in performance on the other two. While we bear in mind the over-confidence in the variability estimates (c.f. Bengio & Grandvalet (2004)), this experiment does support our theory regarding the power of RP-GNNs.

kk-ary RP-GNN experiments

Next we address two complementary questions related to the kk-ary dependency models – evaluating f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} on kk-node induced subgraphs – discussed in section 2.3.3. First, proposition 2.3 shows that expressive power is lost as kk decreases. Second, the computational complexity should also decrease with kk. To empirically evaluate these, we implement kk-ary RP with f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} represented by the model of Duvenaud et al. (2015) in equation 10. We consider k=10,20,30,40,50k=10,20,30,40,50, where the percentage of molecules with greater than kk atoms are: 98.18%, 63.71%, 22.30%, 7.71%, 3.59% for HIV, 99.93%, 75.33%, 12.30%, 0.03%, 0.00% for MUV, and 78.07%, 33.63%, 10.39%, 3.90%, 1.97% for Tox21.

The kk-ary RP-GNN is trained using π\pi-SGD, and evaluated using five random train/validation/test splits. Results are shown in Table 2 and figures 4, 5, and 6 in the Supplementary Material. With the Tox21 dataset, we see a steady improvement in performance and computation as kk increases but the benefits level off around k=30k=30. In particular, k-ary with k=10k=10 is 25% faster than the baseline with AUC 0.687 (±\pm0.005 std), with k=20k=20 being 10% faster with AUC 0.755 (±\pm0.003 std), and k=30k=30 about 5% faster with AUC 0.775 (±\pm0.011 std), where (±x​ std)(\pm x\text{ std}) indicates the standard deviation over 5 bootstrapped runs (see also figure 4). For the other two datasets, both predictive performance and computation do not vary significantly with kk. Overall, the molecules are quite small, thus we do not expect to observe dramatic large computational gains with smaller kk.

RP with CNNs and RNNs.

We now explore 2020-ary RP with f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} as a CNN, learned with π\pi-SGD. At each forward step, we run a DFS from a different randomly-selected vertex to obtain a 20×20×1420\times 20\times 14 subtensor of 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}} (there are 14 edge features), which we feed through two iterations of conv→ReLU→MaxPool\text{conv}\rightarrow\text{ReLU}\rightarrow\text{MaxPool} to obtain a representation 𝒉𝑨{\bm{h}}_{{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}} of 𝑨{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}. The vertex attributes are fed through an MLP and concatenated with 𝒉𝑨{\bm{h}}_{{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}}, to obtain a representation 𝒉G{\bm{h}}_{G} of the graph which in turn is fed through an MLP to obtain the predicted class (as in equation 3). Zero padding was used to account for the variable-sized molecules. Twenty permutations were sampled at inference time. Table 2 shows that the CNN f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} underperforms in all tasks.

We also consider RP with an RNN as f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$} learned with π\pi-SGD, again starting with a DFS to yield a |V||V| ×\times |V||V| ×\times 14 subtensor. For f⇀\mathstrut\mkern 2.5muf\mkern-11.0mu\raise 6.88889pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}, we treat the edge features of a given vertex as a sequence: for vertex vv, we apply an LSTM to the sequence (𝑨v,1,⋅,𝑨v,2,⋅,…,𝑨v,|V|,⋅)({\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{v,1,\cdot},{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{v,2,\cdot},\ldots,{\bm{\mathsfit{A}}}_{v,|V|,\cdot}) and extract the long-term state. We also take the vertex attributes and pass them through an MLP. The long term state and output of the MLP are concatenated, ultimately forming a representation for every vertex (and its neighborhood) which we view as a second sequence. We apply a second LSTM and again extract the long term state, which can be denoted 𝒉G{\bm{h}}_{G}, the embedding of the graph. Last, 𝒉G{\bm{h}}_{G} is forwarded through an MLP yielding a class prediction. Twenty permutations were sampled at inference time. Variability was quantified with 5 random train/val/test splits for both neural network based models. Interestingly, Table 2 shows that the RP-RNN approach performs reasonably well in the Tox21 dataset, while underperforming in other datasets. Future work is needed to determine those tasks for which the RNN and CNN approaches are better suited.

5 Conclusions

In this work, we proposed a framework, Relational Pooling (RP), for graph classification and regression tasks. Our RP framework is shown to give ideal most powerful, though intractable, graph representations. We then propose a number of approaches to tractably approximate this ideal. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that RP allows a WL-GNN to be more expressive than its WL test, and permits neural network architectures like RNNs and CNNs to be brought to such problems. In our experiments, we evaluate these on a number of datasets, showing how our framework can be used to improve properties of state-of-the-art methods. Among future directions for theoretical study is to better understand the representational power of our tractable approaches, as well as the trade-offs that they involve.
